extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners, media relations specialists, internal communications managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for setting objectives and evaluating media-relations programs and internal (employee/member) communications, including agenda-setting goals, clipping/content analysis metrics, media selection, reporter-targeting strategies, publication formats, and two-way internal communication principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-setting objectives (communication and message retention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define realistic media-relations objectives as getting the proper message onto the media agenda (communication) and keeping it there long enough for the public to be aware of and retain it (message retention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with the press to place the organization's message on the media agenda; once on the agenda, seek sustained presence so publics will retain the message. After these objectives are met, practitioners have little control over subsequent cognitions, attitudes, or behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration required on media agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: A story must be on the media agenda for some time—about three to five months—before people become thoroughly aware of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan sustained publicity efforts rather than one-off placements; short-lived TV introductions may not affix an issue to the public agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media selection for agenda impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers tend to set the public agenda more than television, which introduces issues but does not stay with them long enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer newspapers and print media for sustained agenda-setting goals; use television for introductions but rely on press that provide ongoing coverage for lasting public awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience involvement moderates media effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all people adopt media agendas equally: the more involved people are with an issue, the less the media affect how important those people think the issue is; people with high need for orientation accept the media agenda more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences by involvement and need-for-orientation; target less-involved or high-orientation publics for agenda-setting messages and use other channels for highly involved publics who seek information actively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build-versus-set agenda (interaction with news sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues are often 'built' by interactions between news sources (organizations, politicians) and journalists rather than simply 'set' by media decisions alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate what organizational spokespersons say with journalists' reporting practices; use credible news sources and story hooks so journalists will report and thereby 'build' the agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of clipping services for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial clipping services collect all articles that mention an organization from specified media so media relations specialists can evaluate frequency and context of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set clear objectives for desired coverage themes and media, and use clipping services (or in-house systems) to collect and present clippings systematically to management as evidence of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-analysis of press clippings (theme frequency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze clippings for how frequently desired themes actually appear in desired media (content analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the themes and target media in advance; use trained coders or a computer (PR DATA example) to count occurrences and produce comparable metrics over time (see Chapter 9 for content-analysis methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone classification of coverage (positive/negative/neutral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify clippings as positive, negative, or neutral and chart results year by year to monitor progress in media relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop coding rules for valence; track trends and use this metric to evaluate whether coverage sentiment aligns with organizational objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal ratio (response to unfavorable stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: When stories are unfavorable, measure the 'rebuttal ratio'—the relative proportion of times the media relations person gets a later rebuttal to an unfavorable article onto the media agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track how often you secure corrective or clarifying coverage after negative pieces; use rebuttal ratio as an indicator of ability to influence the ongoing agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiative ratio (company-initiated vs media-initiated stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the relative number of stories initiated by the company’s media relations people compared to stories initiated by the media themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high proportion of company-initiated stories suggests proactive influence; compare ratios over time to assess whether media specialists are effectively shaping coverage versus merely reacting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message-retention measurement via surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether target publics retain media themes as their own, conduct surveys that measure message retention—recall of the themes stressed in the media—not attitudes or behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design survey questions to test recall of specific themes and content items (see Chapter 9 for sample questions); use results to evaluate whether agenda-setting objectives achieved public awareness/retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor media relations strategies to reporter typologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters vary (enterprising/specialized, passive, institutional); treat different kinds of reporters differently: help enterprising/specialized reporters get complete factual information; make information available and 'put it on the agenda' for passive reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify reporters' beats and motivations (self-interest vs institutional prompts) and adapt pitches: supply depth and data to specialized reporters; provide accessible leads, local angles, and ready-to-use material for passive reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local-angle and gatekeeper considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and gatekeepers often select releases with a local angle or other news values rather than at random.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame releases with local relevance and strong news hooks; research typical gatekeeper preferences for target outlets to improve placement odds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid technical-jargon mismatch with journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Information presented in technical jargon (e.g., after incidents) reduces the likelihood journalists will use it effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate technical information into clear, journalist-friendly language and provide context so reporters can write usable stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set objectives for kind of media coverage desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Media relations managers must set objectives for the kind of media coverage desired and then systematically analyze press clippings to see if those objectives have been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define measurable targets (themes, media, tone, placement) prior to campaign and use clipping/content metrics and surveys to judge success against those objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of in-house content-analysis when budget-constrained
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations that cannot afford commercial firms can perform content analysis themselves; a computer makes calculations easier but is not essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train staff on coding rules, collect clippings systematically, and produce basic frequency and valence counts to assess media relations performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee-publications objectives (socialization and morale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal publications should help develop pride and identification with the organization; build participation in activities that improve efficiency and effectiveness; develop loyalty; humanize management; promote social/recreational activities; and recognize accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align publication content with these objectives rather than filling pages with trivial 'warm maple syrup' items; use publications as part of broader employee-relations strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid press-agentry 'warm maple syrup' content
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-pattern: filling internal publications with baby photos, bowling scores, recipes, and other innocuous material that humanizes but does not inform or engage employees meaningfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor substantive content that helps employees evaluate and understand the organization; reserve human-interest pieces for appropriate balance but not as primary content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose publication format to match objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Different internal publication formats suit different objectives: magazines humanize and convey quality; newspapers provide timely hard news and support symmetric programs; newsletters are simple, fast, and flexible; 'magapapers' bridge news and in-depth treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select format (magazine, newspaper, newsletter, magapaper) based on frequency needs, desired depth, and whether the program emphasizes symmetric two-way communication or managerial messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple internal media channels appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal programs should consider a wide array of media (bulletin boards, daily news sheets, booklets, audiovisuals, videotapes/films, exhibits, open houses, hotlines, closed-circuit TV, paycheck inserts, letters from managers, orientation media, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match channel to message type and audience needs (timeliness, interactivity, reach); don't rely solely on printed house organs when other channels better serve objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal-media content categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Common types of information for internal media include general business and industry information, organizational policy, systems and procedures, day-to-day operating information, public affairs/economic education, marketing/sales information, division-level news, personnel policies, benefits, employee activities, personal development, and job/skill training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure internal media provide information employees need for orientation, effectiveness, and evaluation of management; include training and benefits information to support employee needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on purpose over technique in internal publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-pattern: concentrating on format, style, graphics, layout, and deadlines more than fulfilling a publication's purpose and objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize content and the publication's objectives in planning and evaluation; use good design to support communication goals, not as an end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way symmetric internal communication principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Open, two-way programs should: inform employees ahead of time about changes affecting their jobs; care about how employees feel and be open and honest; give supervisors enough authority; commit to serving the customer; solve major company problems; run a socially responsible organization; provide new products/services to meet competition; place more emphasis on quality than quantity; and communicate openly about management actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt organizational practices that match communications—employees want to know what's going on and to feel that management genuinely cares. These perceptions affect job satisfaction more than technical polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loosen constraints and protect employee voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations should build bridges between managers and the managed so employees can speak out without fear of reprisal; constraints must be loosened if employees are to be satisfied and productive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design internal communications and organizational practices to allow legitimate grievance airing and two-way feedback; failure to do so can lead to disgruntlement and reduces program effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate employee-communication programs relative to organizational structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives of employee relations depend upon the structure of the organization; evaluation should consider whether programs meet needs given that structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess employee-publics (see studies of employee publics), set objectives consistent with organizational type, and use surveys, readership measures, and program metrics to evaluate effectiveness.
